title: The turban in the code
hook: the code asks men to wear a turban; women may choose to

segments.voice: Yesterday, daswandh: a tenth of honest earnings, set aside first for the Guru's cause. Your line was a tenth. Where did your small share go, or where will it go this week? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-six.

Early morning, in front of a mirror. A long strip of cloth, starched or soft, is shaken out and folded lengthwise. One end goes between the teeth to hold it. Then the wrapping starts: around, up, across, pleat by pleat, each layer laid flat over the one before, the hands moving the way hands move after years of doing the same thing. A pin tucked here. A last pass at the front, checked in the mirror, adjusted by a finger's width. Done. It took a few minutes, and the whole day will be lived inside it. Today's word is that cloth.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH, A MIRROR.` → `PLEAT BY PLEAT.` → `A WHOLE DAY INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Dastar is the Sikh turban. The Sikh Rehat Maryada says, in paraphrase, that a Sikh man must wear a turban, and that for a Sikh woman wearing one is optional. Some Sikh women tie a dastar every day; others cover their hair with a long scarf, a chunni. Both are within the code. Why a turban at all? It starts with the hair. Keeping the hair uncut, kesh, is part of the Sikh way, and the code asks Sikhs to keep it. A turban covers it, keeps it clean and tidy, and keeps it with the comb, the kangha, tucked inside. So the dastar isn't decoration on top of the faith. It is how the uncut hair, kept as a gift, is cared for. Then there's what it says. Sikhs speak of the dastar as a crown, given by the Guru. Tradition says that in the world the Gurus knew, a turban could mark rank and nobility. On a Sikh head it is worn by a farmer, a teacher and a surgeon alike. Nobody's turban is a lower one. And a crown carries a weight. A Sikh in a turban can't blend into a crowd. Whatever they do, a stranger may remember it as what a Sikh did. Some Sikhs describe that as the turban's quiet job: a daily reminder to act like someone the Guru crowned. That is why, for Sikhs who wear it, being told to remove it is not a small thing. It isn't a hat. It's part of the self, tied fresh each morning.
screen: `THE CODE: MEN WEAR IT; WOMEN MAY.` · `IT COVERS AND KEEPS THE KESH.` · `A CROWN FOR EVERY HEAD.` · `A CROWN CARRIES A WEIGHT.` · then, large: `CROWNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tie or fold a cloth neatly. Find any piece of fabric near you: a scarf, a towel, a napkin, even a shirt. Shake it out. Fold it slowly, edge to edge, and smooth each fold flat with your palm before you make the next one. No rush. Feel how care goes into each layer. When it's done, set it in your lap, rest your hands on it, and breathe. Notice that something ordinary now looks cared for. The bell holds the time.
Dastar. The Sikh turban: required by the code for men, a choice for women, covering the uncut hair and worn as a crown from the Guru. Today's word.
Your line: crowned. Today, pick one moment when you could slip by unnoticed, and act instead as if someone might remember it as yours. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-six.
